questions: Are your eye movements involuntary and difficult to control?
Do you see the world shaking or moving when this happens?
Do you experience double vision during these episodes?
Did these eye movements begin suddenly?
Have they been present continuously for more than a few days?
Do you have dizziness, spinning, nausea, or trouble walking?
Do you have a new severe headache, weakness, numbness, facial drooping, or difficulty speaking?
Have you had any recent head injury or loss of consciousness?
Have you recently had a fever, infection, or vaccination?
Have you used alcohol, recreational drugs, or any new prescription or over-the-counter medication recently?
Do you have a history of thyroid disease, multiple sclerosis, seizures, or other neurological illness?
Do you have reduced vision, eye pain, or new sensitivity to light?
Can you deliberately reproduce the eye movements on command?
Do the movements continue when you are looking straight ahead and trying to keep your eyes still?

results: 1. Comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic examination with visual acuity, pupils, ocular alignment, ductions and versions, and fundus examination.
cranial nerve examination: internuclear ophthalmoplegia with impaired left eye adduction; ipsilesional torsional nystagmus; alternating skew deviation
fundoscopy: normal
adduction in horizontal gaze (each eye): full
vertical gaze and convergence: normal
pupil size and light reaction: equal and reactive
2. Alternate-cover and prism-cover testing at distance and near, including measurements in different gaze positions.
skew deviation / alternating cover test: skew deviation with LATERAL ALTERNATION - right eye hypotropic, left eye hypertropic
3. Examination for ocular-motor fatigability, saccadic intrusions, convergence spasm, and gaze-evoked nystagmus.
nystagmus: direction and whether it changes with gaze: ipsilesional torsional nystagmus
smooth pursuit and saccades: normal
vertical gaze and convergence: normal
4. Bedside vestibular and cerebellar examination, including head-impulse, nystagmus, test-of-skew, gait, and coordination testing.
coordination examination (limb and truncal): left-sided limb and truncal ataxia
head impulse test: normal - no corrective saccade
nystagmus: direction and whether it changes with gaze: ipsilesional torsional nystagmus
skew deviation / alternating cover test: skew deviation with LATERAL ALTERNATION - right eye hypotropic, left eye hypertropic
limb and truncal ataxia: left-sided limb ataxia
gait and tandem walking: normal
5. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits with and without contrast, including diffusion-weighted imaging focused on the brainstem and cerebellum.
MRI brain with gadolinium: left rostral pontine and caudal mesencephalic infarcts without enhancement
MRI diffusion-weighted sequences: restricted diffusion in the left rostral pons and caudal mesencephalon extending along the paramedian line to the midline
MRI brain with DWI: LEFT rostral pontine infarct and a caudal mesencephalic infarct extending along the paramedian line to the midline
MRI sella and orbits: normal pituitary and orbits
6. Magnetic resonance angiography of the head and neck.
CT / MR angiography (posterior circulation): TOP-OF-THE-BASILAR OCCLUSION; thrombectomy was deferred as he was well preserved
CT / MR angiography (circle of Willis): normal / non-contributory
7. Ice-pack test and sustained upgaze testing for ocular myasthenia gravis.
not performed / not available
8. Serum acetylcholine-receptor antibodies and MuSK antibodies.
acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies: normal
anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies: negative
9. Video-oculography during primary gaze, eccentric gaze, convergence, and fixation.
video-oculography / eye-movement recording: ipsilesional torsional nystagmus with internuclear ophthalmoplegia and alternating skew deviation
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Acute left pontomesencephalic ischemic stroke caused by top-of-the-basilar artery occlusion (basilar artery thrombosis/embolism), producing internuclear ophthalmoplegia, alternating skew deviation, torsional nystagmus, and left-sided ataxia.

ALTERNATIVE: Basilar artery dissection with thrombotic occlusion and brainstem infarction.

ALTERNATIVE: Cardioembolic basilar artery occlusion.

ALTERNATIVE: Demyelinating brainstem lesion causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
